input.goal: Review two independent Marionette v5 guides for correct ownership, scope and verifiable teaching. Read-only review.
input.currentPlan: Deliver existing UI mount boundary and synchronous hash routing. Async transitions are explicitly scoped as remaining policy, no router framework or helpers. Core Region.destroy leaves mount; app.destroy is async. Browser tests and installed packaging running.
input.diffSummary: Adds two guides and executes their actual fences locally/installed and in Chromium Firefox WebKit.
input.openQuestions: Check cleanup claims, async host caveats, usefulness beyond sample, routing policy assumptions. Identify confirmed defects or missing decisive checks.

result.verdict: Needs changes. Ownership and scope are right, and the synchronous claims in both guides are backed by executed fences, including Chromium, Firefox and WebKit runs of the documented code. However, the existing-ui "asynchronous readiness" section states library behavior that nothing in this change checks. A few other stated behaviors are also unasserted. No confirmed product bugs; the gaps are in the docs and tests.
blockingIssues: existing-ui.md, 'Host a feature with asynchronous readiness': this section states Marionette behavior with no example and no check. It says destroy() cancels pending activation through the lifecycle signal, that no late root appears after unmounting during prepareStart, and that destroy() resolves once teardown is complete. Its own 'Check the boundary' section tells readers to 'unmount during preparation and verify no late root appears', but the guide's checks never do this. Either add a fence (an Application with region:{el}, a pending prepareStart, destroy mid-start, then assert the rejected or cancelled start, an empty mount and a connected host) plus its check, or cut the section to a short pointer to api/application.md, where those claims are presumably already tested.
risks: routing.md focuses the heading on the first start, including direct links. Moving focus on initial page load is widely discouraged, and the browser test locks this in with toBeFocused on the first render. Consider focusing only on later navigations, or say plainly that initial-load focus is a choice the reader must make.

showRoute is public but not guarded after stop: this.getView() is undefined, so a direct call throws. The test depends on the listener being removed rather than on the method being safe. That's fine for a sample, but someone copying it could hit this.

Browser test: the '// A removed listener must not try to access the destroyed shell' step sets location.hash while the app is stopped. hashchange fires asynchronously, and nothing proves it fired before start() re-added the listener. If it lands afterwards, currentRoute de-dupes it, so the step can pass without testing what the comment says. The synthetic routeCalls===0 check just before it is the one that actually decides this; the later step is redundant or misleading.

Node check: after `await app.stop()`, the check dispatches hashchange and asserts app.getView() === undefined. In jsdom an exception thrown inside a listener goes to the virtual console and does not fail the test, so a leaked listener would pass in Node. Only the browser test catches it.

Node routing check assumes the starting hash is empty (it asserts 'Home') and leaves the global URL at '#about' (replaceState) without resetting it. This leaks into other guide checks if they share a jsdom window.
Playwright goBack/goForward across fragment-only entries has a history of flakiness in WebKit. Watch CI for intermittent failures before treating one as a product bug.

existing-ui browser test: the retained-button click after destroy can't tell apart the two protections, View events being undelegated and the Region's stopListening. The claim in the guide holds either way, but a regression in either layer alone would go unnoticed.
incorrectAssumptions: 'Selecting the same route keeps the current page': in a browser, clicking a link to the current fragment does not fire hashchange at all, so the currentRoute guard never runs in that case. The guard really matters for direct showRoute() calls, which is how both tests exercise it. The wording implies a user-facing behavior the code doesn't produce; reword it or drop the claim.

'A synchronous cleanup hook must initiate destruction immediately and arrange error handling' assumes destroy() can reject. If core destroy() never rejects, this advice is noise. If it can reject, the guide should name the failure mode.
missingTests: document.title is never asserted in either the Node or the browser routing checks, though the guide says each destination updates it.
An async existing-ui scenario: destroy during a pending prepareStart, then assert the host is still connected, no root was rendered and the start outcome is observable. Needed if the section stays.
Browser existing-ui test does not call destroy() twice. Only the Node check verifies 'repeated cleanup is safe'.
'Removing DOM alone does not destroy a View or Application' is stated but never exercised. Remove the host element, assert the View is not destroyed, then clean up.

Routing: no test for a bare '#' or empty hash mapping to home against a '#home' link, i.e. that loading '' and then clicking Home doesn't re-render. Node covers this implicitly only if the initial hash is empty.
Node routing check should reset the hash (replaceState to '' or the original) in its teardown.
simplifications: Drop the post-stop `location.hash = '#about'` / waitForFunction step in the browser routing test. The synthetic hashchange routeCalls===0 check already decides listener removal; just set the hash before start().

Replace existing-ui's async prose section with two sentences and a link to application.md, unless you're prepared to add a fence for it. That keeps the guide within its synchronous scope, matching how routing.md scopes out async.
Consider a single `if (!this.isRunning()) return;` (or equivalent) in showRoute rather than relying only on listener removal, if you want the sample to be safe to copy. This is optional.
nextSteps: Resolve the existing-ui async section: add a fence plus check, or cut it to a link.
Add document.title assertions to both routing checks.
Decide the focus policy for initial load and make the guide and browser test agree with it.
Fix the 'same route' wording, remove the non-decisive post-stop hash step, and reset the hash in the Node routing check.
Re-run the Chromium, Firefox and WebKit guide specs and the installed-package run several times to check for WebKit history flakiness.
